meta.title: Who really said "in the zone"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The phrase's earliest known appearance is Arthur Ashe's diary entry of 22 February 1974 — but his own wording shows the slang was already on the tour.
meta.ogDescription: Arthur Ashe wrote it down first, in his 1974 tour diary. Whether he coined it is another question. Sourced, dated, honestly hedged.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: The earliest documented use of the phrase is Ashe’s own diary entry of 22 February 1974, printed in Arthur Ashe: Portrait in Motion (with Frank Deford), where he writes of Björn Borg that “he is in what we call the zone.” Quote Investigator ↗ found no earlier evidence — but note Ashe’s own wording, “what we call the zone,” which presents the term as slang already circulating among players.

source.excerpt: … he is in what we call the zone.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ identifies the 22 February 1974 diary entry as the earliest evidence and quotes it in full, citing p. 201 of the Ballantine Books edition of Arthur Ashe: Portrait in Motion.
The book itself is catalogued by the Internet Archive ↗ as Arthur Ashe with Frank Deford, Houghton Mifflin, Boston, 1975.
The Arthur Ashe Legacy project at UCLA ↗ lists the same title and imprint among his books, confirming the diary is genuinely his.

Quote Investigator’s later citations — a Dallas Morning News piece in May 1975 and a United Press International story in March 1976 — show the phrase spreading outward from tennis with the Twilight Zone explanation attached.
source.excerptNote: In the same entry Ashe adds a parenthetical gloss, tracing the term to “twilight zone” and translating it as, more or less, another world.

source.rightsNote: The wording comes from Arthur Ashe: Portrait in Motion, first published in 1975 — well after the 1931 United States public-domain cutoff — so the diary text remains in copyright. Only the short phrase itself, too brief to be protectable on its own, circulates freely.

author.name: Arthur Ashe
author.heading: About Arthur Ashe
author.metaLine: 1943–1993 · American tennis champion, diarist & civil-rights advocate
author.bio: Arthur Ashe (born 10 July 1943 in Richmond, Virginia; died 6 February 1993) won three Grand Slam singles titles — the US Open in 1968, the Australian Open in 1970 and Wimbledon in 1975 — the first Black man to win any of them. Between Wimbledon 1973 and Wimbledon 1974 he kept a running audio diary of life on tour, published in 1975 as Portrait in Motion: The Arthur Ashe Diary, written with the sportswriter Frank Deford. That book is where the sporting sense of “the zone” first appears in print.

copyAttribution: "…he is in what we call the zone." — Arthur Ashe, diary entry of 22 February 1974, published in Arthur Ashe: Portrait in Motion (with Frank Deford), Houghton Mifflin, 1975. Earliest known evidence of the phrase, per Quote Investigator. Verified at quotle.info.

misattribution.heading: What gets said about this one
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Ashe is unusually well documented — but three claims regularly travel with it that the sources do not support.

items.why: Ashe’s sentence is “he is in what we call the zone” — he is glossing an in-group term for readers, not minting one. Quote Investigator ↗ credits him with popularising the expression and says he may have taken part in coining it, while noting the origin remains uncertain.

That derivation is Ashe’s aside in the same 1974 entry, repeated in a 1976 United Press International story quoted by Quote Investigator ↗. It is what players believed, not an etymology established by lexicographers — Wiktionary ↗ offers no origin for the idiom.

items.who: Quote cards crediting a bare “in the zone” to Ashe
items.why: Aggregator pages pin the phrase to Ashe with no book, page or date. The actual citation is narrow and checkable: a diary entry dated 22 February 1974, printed in Arthur Ashe: Portrait in Motion ↗, written with Frank Deford.

misattribution.truthLine: Ashe is the first person known to have written the phrase down, and he wrote it about Björn Borg — but he presented it as tennis-tour slang, and Quote Investigator ↗ stops short of naming a coiner.

context.heading: How a tennis diary gave sport its favourite state of mind
lead: Ashe recorded his 1973–74 season onto tape as he went — airports, locker rooms, hotel beds — and Frank Deford shaped the recordings into a published diary. The entry for 22 February 1974 is a loss: a young Björn Borg beat him, and Ashe reached for a piece of locker-room shorthand to explain why. The kid, he said, was in the zone.

Ashe glossed the term himself, tracing it to The Twilight Zone — the Rod Serling series that ran on CBS from 1959 to 1964 — and rendering it as roughly ‘another world.’ That gloss is Ashe’s explanation, not an independently established etymology, but it is the first time anyone is known to have written the phrase down and said what it meant.
context.detailsSummary: What happened to the phrase afterwards
detailsBody: Quote Investigator’s chronology shows the term spreading out of tennis over the following years: a Dallas Morning News piece in May 1975, a United Press International story carried in the Port Arthur News in March 1976 that likewise linked the expression to the science-fiction series, then sightings in the Centre Daily Times (December 1978), the Trenton Evening Times (December 1979) and World Tennis magazine (February 1982).
Today it is simply general English: Wiktionary ↗ defines it as a state of focused concentration in which one shuts out everything irrelevant, and offers no etymology at all.
